items.summary: NANOROBOT-ENHANCED DIGITAL TWINS OF BRAIN STATE AT THE LIMIT A multiscale, uncertainty-aware research atlas on microrobotic observations, neural inverse problems, active model discrimination and the limits of computational brain twins. This research monograph asks whether additional microscale observations or strictly bounded reversible experiments can distinguish competing neural-state models that explain conventional measurements equally well. The twin is explicitly defined as a versioned scientific belief, not a digital person, a mind reader or a clinically validated instrument. Its objective is not maximum model complexity but improved identifiability, calibrated prediction under new conditions and faithful retention of failed hypotheses. The work develops five layers: multiscale neural and microenvironment state representation; posterior equivalence and prior sensitivity; non-clinical safe experimental design; frozen-version forking, rollback and reference ancestry; and blind prospective validation against classical state-space systems and independently specified alternatives. Its research architecture includes 30 distinct mathematical derivation plates linked to later chapters, 82 chapters with five independently paginated research sections apiece, 200 detailed Research Gates and 33 revisable Phoenix Answer Embryos. A DOI evidence ledger identifies existing support for brain modeling, latent neural dynamics, experiment design and preclinical microrobot tracking while preventing those sources from being mistaken for evidence of the proposed integrated system. Key research questions include: Can two equally accurate virtual brains be separated by a small, permissible observation? How can the effect of a measurement itself be separated from neural change? When does a prior dominate the inferred brain state? Can the model predict unseen function rather than reconstruct a training signal? Can another laboratory reproduce a rejected twin and safely return to an earlier version? SCIENTIFIC STATUS AND LIMITATIONS This is a forward-looking, non-clinical research synthesis and experimental hypothesis architecture. It provides no personal medical advice, patient-specific interpretations or instruction to deliver neural interventions. Existing murine microrobot tracking and virtual-brain modeling studies do not establish autonomous neural nanorobot readout, human safety, privacy-sensitive mind inference or therapeutic efficacy. Proposed formulas, experiments, research gates and answer embryos are not newly validated biological laws or executed experiments. The work keeps independent safety vetoes, privacy, external reproducibility and explicit model retirement as first-class constraints. Research questions remain open to refutation, correction and reconstruction by future human and AI researchers.

items.summary: Recent advances in deep learning have significantly improved underwater acoustic vessel recognition. However, existing publicly available datasets are typically limited in scale, hindering large-scale representation learning and downstream task evaluation. To address this limitation, we introduce ONCship, a large-scale underwater acoustic dataset comprising 4521 hours of curated recordings from Ocean Networks Canada (ONC) hydrophones and Automatic Identification System (AIS) data. We evaluate the proposed dataset across three tasks: self-supervised representation learning, vessel-type classification, and MMSI-Level Vessel Classification. Experiments on DeepShip and ShipsEar demonstrate the effectiveness of ONCship for acoustic representation learning, with joint pre-training on ONCship and AudioSet achieving a classification accuracy of 62.45% on DeepShip through linear probing. Furthermore, incorporating ONCship as auxiliary training data improves downstream vessel-type classification performance. Beyond conventional vessel-type classification, we further investigate MMSI-Level Vessel Classification, treating each vessel as a distinct identity. Experimental results show that models fine-tuned with different loss functions achieve Top-1 accuracies exceeding 53% and Top-5 accuracies approaching 69%, demonstrating the feasibility of distinguishing individual vessels through MMSI-Level Vessel Classification. Overall, ONCship provides a valuable resource for underwater acoustic representation learning and vessel recognition, while its rich vessel-level metadata enables further exploration of MMSI-Level Vessel Classification.

items.summary: This technical note documents a conditional mathematical correspondence between the static spatial kernel used in conventional electromagnetic potential theory and the fixed-source gravitational potential in Lisa Doumbouya’s Harmonic Physics programme. Under supplied three-dimensional Euclidean geometry, spherical symmetry and stated boundary conditions, the derivation gives the static Green function 1/(4πr). Applying the existing gravitational source normalization yields the potential −μ/r, whose radial derivative gives the inward acceleration −μ/r². The note distinguishes potential, field amplitude, intensity, acceleration and optical measurement conversion, keeping geometric normalization separate from the distance exponent. The optical phase-ruler results are reviewed alongside the GRACE-FO forward forecasts. Calibrated reconstruction using measured phase retained micrometre-scale agreement with processed microwave ranging, while some forward models produced much larger errors. These results do not establish exponential error growth or identify a unique physical cause. The correspondence uses established mathematics and remains conditional on the supplied geometry, source calibration and physical interpretation. It does not establish an electromagnetic mechanism of gravity or derive spatial geometry from foundational Phase. The note includes the analytical proof, assumptions, evidence boundaries and requirements for a subsequent physical test. No new experimental data are introduced.
items.title: Inverse Radius Kernel and Optical Phase Registration

items.summary: LONGITUDINAL DEVICE MIGRATION AND MEANING CONTINUITY AT THE LIMIT Device Replacement × Model Bridging × Control Semantics STARLI RESEARCH WORKS | INSTITUTE XXIV | FLAGSHIP 24 Feng Cheng-en 33 × Starli Research Works This research monograph investigates a deceptively difficult question in long-term brain–computer interfaces: when sensors, acquisition electronics, firmware, electrode geometry, or decoding models change, what would justify the claim that a user's task-grounded control meaning has been preserved? Numerical signal alignment alone cannot establish continuity of intention. Two systems may encode different signals while supporting the same functional command, or produce nearly identical latent representations while mapping to incompatible actions. The volume formulates meaning continuity as a conditional, falsifiable engineering and scientific hypothesis. It connects device-specific observation models, neural recording instability, task and action ontologies, paired old/new sensing periods, latent manifold bridging, longitudinal recalibration, calibrated abstention, functional validation, and an accessible right to reject the proposed migration. Its central commitment is that no amount of predictive accuracy can compensate for invalid authorization, an unverified physical reference, or loss of independent control. The research atlas comprises thirty connected mathematical derivations, eighty-two research chapters, and 410 independently paginated chapter sections that examine observables, inverse explanations, discriminating experiments, uncertainty and noncompensable safeguards, and independent requalification. Two hundred detailed Research Gates propose future falsification and handoff programs, while thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos preserve revisable candidate approaches rather than immutable conclusions. A claim-scoped DOI evidence ledger connects the study to published work on neural recording drift, decoder adaptation, manifold alignment, longitudinal neural interfaces, speech BCIs, user preferences, and neurotechnology ethics. The book is designed for both human researchers and future AI research systems. Its formulas, chapter cross-links, DOI anchors, competing models, negative-result requirements, and successor-focused research cards provide structured entry points for independent reconstruction and informed disagreement. The visual presentation combines ivory pages, navy and teal typography, and large gold mathematical plates, while mathematical expressions are also recorded in searchable source notation and a separate Excel reference index. This is a prospective, nonclinical research architecture. It does not report new patient experiments, demonstrate safe autonomous human neurovascular microrobots, establish a universal device-migration system, or claim continuity of private thoughts, consciousness, or personal identity. Scientific benefit remains conditional on explicit task definitions, qualified device evidence, legitimate permissions, external validation, and the successor's freedom to reject a failed bridge. Research question: What should remain invariant when an interface changes, and who has the authority to say that its meaning has changed?

items.summary: Fisher information metric tensors for the 41 held-out SONICOM test subjects, as used in “Evaluating Spatial Discriminability Preservation in HRTF Upsampling Using Fisher Information” (D. Bassett). Code and reproduction instructions: https://github.com/domfrbassett/fisher-rao-hrtf-upsampling What the tensors are At each of the 793 directions of the SONICOM grid, the 2×2 tensor g = JᵀΣ⁻¹J describes how well the auditory cues separate that direction from its neighbours. J is the spatial Jacobian of the cues: Barumerli monaural PGE features, ILD and MaxIACCe-transformed ITD, each fitted with real spherical harmonics. Σ holds the cue noise (σ_mon = 1.25 dB, σ_ILD = 1 dB, σ_ITD = 0.569). All fields are low-pass filtered at 16 kHz before the cues are extracted. The tensor is expressed in a local tangent basis u₁ = a × r, u₂ = r × u₁, where a = z, or y when |r_z| > 0.9, and its units are d′² per rad². Contents metric_tensors.zip has one folder per subject, metric_tensors/subject_####/ , containing 25 files per subject (1,025 in total): reference_metric_tensor.mat : the dense measured HRTF. <METHOD>_N###_metric_tensor.mat : one file per reconstruction. There are six methods: SUpDEq_SH , SUpDEq_MCA , SUpDEq_NN_MCA_6dB (SUpDEq-Natural-MCA in the paper), SUpDEq_Bary_MCA_6dB , RANF and FSP_AE . Each is reconstructed from N = 100, 19, 5 and 3 retained directions. The 164 natural-neighbour and barycentric files at N = 5 and 3 have status “ not_applicable ”. The interpolation is undefined for those masks, so these files carry no tensors. Variables in each file: metricTensor : the tensors at SH order 6 [2×2×793]. familyGram : per-cue-family Gram matrices JᵀJ before noise weighting, at SH orders 4, 6 and 8 [2×2×793×3 families×3 orders]. They let you recompute the tensors with other noise values or SH orders. In reconstruction files only: crossFamilyGram : the unsymmetrised cross terms J_refᵀ J_recon, same layout as familyGram . airmByDirection : the pointwise AIRM discrepancy from the reference. Metadata: coordinates (Cartesian and azimuth/elevation in degrees), cue band, noise values (reference files only), status (“ completed ” or “ not_applicable ”) and, for not-applicable files, a message giving the reason. SHA256SUMS.txt lists a checksum for every file. Format and use The files are MATLAB v7.3 (HDF5), so MATLAB, h5py or any HDF5 reader can open them. Note that h5py reverses MATLAB’s axis order. scripts/fisher_lib.py in the repository reads them and recomputes tensors, AIRM and thresholds from the Gram matrices. To rerun the analysis scripts, unzip into results/evaluation/ so the subject folders sit in results/evaluation/metric_tensors/ . Provenance Produced with run_evaluation("tensors") from the repository above. The values are numerically identical to the tensor files behind results/evaluation/full_evaluation_summary.csv ; this run additionally stores the cross terms. The tensors are derived from the SONICOM HRTF Dataset (Engel et al., J. Audio Eng. Soc. 71(5), 2023, doi:10.17743/jaes.2022.0066). The SONICOM HRTFs are released under the MIT licence. This work develops research begun for the author’s B.Sc. dissertation at Birmingham City University.
items.title: Fisher information metric tensors for 'Evaluating Spatial Discriminability Preservation in HRTF Upsampling Using Fisher Information'

items.summary: This metadata entry record constitutes the fourth, concluding installment of a foundational cosmological paper tetralogy (complementing the preceding works registered under DOI:10.5281/zenodo.22763071, DOI:10.5281/zenodo.23153625, and DOI:10.5281/zenodo.23209528).  In this final paper, we formalize the self-consistent microphysical scenarios and underlying relativistic field equations governing primordial lepto- and baryogenesis within a strictly deterministic, parameter-free Extremal Quantum Black Hole (EQBH) cosmological bounce framework occurring immediately post-turnaround. Unified Lepto- and Baryogenesis Dynamics: Tracing the sub-Planckian three-body beta decays of dark-sector super-neutrons that seed the primary lepton background and active neutrino mass scales (m_nu_a ≈ 0.05 eV, m_nu_s ≈ 0.009 eV), paired with a laser-driven CP-violation mechanism that secures the observed baryon asymmetry. 2. items.summary: SELF-CALIBRATING NANO-NEURAL INTERFACES AND REFERENCE LINEAGE AT THE LIMIT Built-In References × Drift Attribution × Independent Functional Requalification STARLI / Institute XXIII / Research Flagship 17 PUBLICATION DESCRIPTION When a long-running neural interface changes, is the cause the sensor, the surrounding tissue, or the decoder? An adaptive algorithm can restore predictive accuracy while obscuring the physical origin of its own correction. This book proposes a rigorous, falsifiable architecture for self-calibrating nano-neural interfaces that must retain the scientific history of every reference and every update. Its central axiom is that self-calibration does not imply self-certification: measurement claims, permission to change, electrode safety and functional benefit demand independent evidence. The first coupling is the existence of physically traceable internal references that can be challenged against electrically and temporally independent standards. The second is a source-aware drift-diagnostic process that distinguishes electronics gain, electrode-tissue transfer, tissue-like surrogate changes, changing source signals and model/feature drift, explicitly recording instances of nonidentifiability. The third is external functional requalification, which can reject an apparently successful update after hidden-domain testing, material or reference replacement, loss of selectivity, missing raw observations, or inability to reproduce the frozen predecessor. This research monograph is divided into seven causal layers and 82 chapters. Five major subsections of each chapter are assigned independent pages, yielding 410 separately paginated technical essays. Thirty gold mathematical derivations are linked from chapter-opening equations to discriminating experiments. The mathematics includes augmented state-space observability, nonlinear observation functions, source-separation Jacobians, Kalman innovations, impedance spectroscopy, covariance propagation, change-point statistics, conformal coverage, selective risk, hard-veto constrained update eligibility, reference-bridge covariance, exact rollback and cross-laboratory requalification. A displayed formula is a candidate analytical instrument with stated dimensions and assumptions, not a discovered biological law. Two hundred detailed Research Gates are preserved at the rear: 82 interrogate source identifiability, another 82 challenge independent physical and evidential hard vetoes, and 36 require third-party reconstruction of a frozen reference history. Thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos propose revisable architectures, beginning with the Neural Interface Calibration Passport. The Passport ties an interface's physical identity to the raw analog and digitized record, calibrated unit chain, hardware reference ancestors, model and feature checksums, reasons for changing any reference, failed updates, revoked permissions, blinded requalification and rollback. These are proposed evidence structures, not commercially validated devices. The DOI bibliography contains 18 unique external research records covering chronic intracortical signal instability, low-dimensional BCI stabilization, decoder adaptation, long-term electrode-tissue behavior, complex impedance metrology, electrochemical reference limits, neural interface materials and conformal uncertainty under covariate shift. Selected publisher and PubMed pages were consulted for source metadata. Their findings cannot establish efficacy of the new self-calibration architecture; source-specific claims and independent replication would be necessary.

items.summary: Large audio-language models (LALMs) are fast becoming a general interface to sound, yet how far their broad pretraining carries into specialized domains remains largely open. Vessel monitoring, maritime safety, and ocean sensing all depend on recognizing underwater signals, but to our knowledge LALMs have not been systematically evaluated on them. Annotated recordings are costly to collect, and a faithful synthetic alternative has to bring together many interacting factors: the structure of detection pulses, communication waveforms, and ship-radiated noise, and the sound-speed profile, geometry, and multipath propagation through which each reaches the receiver. We address this by proposing \textbf{UA-Bench}, to our knowledge the first large-scale benchmark for evaluating LALMs on underwater acoustic signal recognition. It comprises 375,051 audio records that couple parameterized sources with modeled propagation, so that every record can be traced to the conditions that produced it. The records span these three signal families, and each carries a three-level label hierarchy (13 leaf classes), a templated multi-turn dialogue, and source and channel metadata. We evaluate on a balanced 2,600-record subset with a gated coarse-to-fine protocol that locates each error at source routing, fine-grained classification, or output format, and add a paired silent-audio control to test whether the waveform is actually used. Nine open LALMs, evaluated without task-specific adaptation, reach only 2.0\%--13.1\% leaf accuracy, against a random reference of 7.7\%. The waveform helps source routing far more than leaf recognition (for one model, +29.5 versus +2.3 points over silence), and just four models gain reliably at the leaf level, by at most 4.7 points. UA-Bench thus gives a reference point for these models, and its released training partition supports follow-up adaptation work.
items.title: UA-Bench: Benchmarking Large Audio-Language Models on Underwater Acoustic Recognition

items.summary: Adaptive modulation and coding (AMC) improves the spectral efficiency of underwater acoustic (UWA) links, but its feedback is inevitably stale: sound propagates slowly, and by the time channel state information (CSI) arrives, the fast time-varying multipath channel has moved on. Predictive link adaptation therefore needs more than a point forecast: it needs a distribution over each candidate action's consequences. We propose PRB-WM, a physics-regularized Beta world model for predictive per-subcarrier link adaptation on real time-varying UWA channels. A persistence-anchored stochastic latent-space dynamics model learns how the channel evolves; a counterfactual outcome head evaluates, for every candidate modulation and coding scheme (MCS), a Beta-binomial distribution of bit errors on shared imagined futures; and a chance-constrained receding-horizon model predictive controller maximizes expected spectral efficiency subject to a bounded probability of violating the bit error rate (BER) target. To the best of our knowledge, PRB-WM is the first world model for UWA communications. In closed-loop replay of six measured sea-trial links from the public UWA Channel Library against a 24-method pool spanning the full methodological spectrum, PRB-WM attains a mean goodput 87% above the strongest baseline, ranks first on all six time-varying links at the longest lookahead, and is the only method whose realized frame risk decreases systematically with lookahead, meeting the BER-violation contract where no baseline does. Ablations confirm that rollout sampling dispersion is essential to the chance constraint and that the physics anchor is necessary for trainability.
items.title: PRB-WM: Physics-Regularized Beta World Models for Predictive Link Adaptation on Real Time-Varying Underwater Acoustic Channels

items.summary: Region means and contrasts with a full error budget, correlated shift errors, error bars for shot noise, a faster fit_map , two tutorials, and three fixes. Added region_mean(coefficients, dw1, dw2, sigma1, sigma2, mask, *, shift_correlation=None, ref_sigma=None) and region_contrast(coefficients, dw1, dw2, sigma1, sigma2, mask_a, mask_b, *, shift_correlation=None) , returning a RegionEstimate : the mean strain and density of a map region, or region A minus region B, with the error split into shift noise (averages down over pixels), calibration (from a two-mode CalibrationResult ; does not average down) and reference frequencies ( ref_sigma ; does not average down, and cancels exactly in a contrast). region_mean also tests whether the pixels agree within their error bars (chi-square with 2 (N - 1) degrees of freedom, the same in shift space and in (strain, density) space) and reports the pixel spread. Validated against the mean and per-pixel covariances of SeparationModel.invert , separation_with_calibration , finite differences of a re-solve, and seeded Monte Carlo over 400 trials that repeat the calibration, the map noise and the reference error (spread within 12 % of the reported error bars). Propagation as in JCGM 100:2008 (GUM), 5.2.2, Eq. (13). SeparationModel.invert(..., shift_correlation=None) : the correlation of the two shift errors (from a joint fit) enters the error bars through the full 2 x 2 shift covariance. Zero gives the old result bit for bit. On 400 repeats of two overlapping E' + A'1 peaks the density error bar without the correlation is 27 % above the actual spread; with it, it matches (tutorial 2). separation_with_calibration passes it through. MapFitResult.shift_correlation : the correlation of the two shift errors per pixel (the joint fit's value, 0 for separate window fits, NaN where masked). noise="varying" in fit_lorentzian , fit_two_modes and fit_map : error bars from the heteroskedasticity-consistent ("sandwich") covariance of H. White, Econometrica 48, 817 (1980), for spectra whose noise level changes along the axis, as shot noise does. Fitted values are unchanged. On 600 seeded Poisson spectra the center scatter is 1.7 times the default error bar and within 10 % of the new one; checked also against an independent finite-difference sandwich (relative 1e-5). The default, noise="constant" , is unchanged. README example 18 (shot noise) and a "Tutorials" section. Fixed calibrate_lever_arms , plan_calibration and design_references judged identifiability from the raw singular values of the design, which depends on the units. Before: the six-state design of the tests with the density in cm^-2 raised ValueError: reference states are collinear ... ( plan_calibration returned identifiable=False ). After: it gives the arms of the fit in 1e13 cm^-2, rescaled (A'1 density arm -2.2798e-13 per cm^-2 against -2.2798 per 1e13 cm^-2; relative 1e-10). The test is now made on the design with unit-length columns (also with fit_offset=True ). Test: test_calibration_does_not_depend_on_the_density_unit , test_planning_does_not_depend_on_the_density_unit . bayesian_map_inversion(..., fill_masked=True) : the same unit dependence in its pooled-information check. items.summary: MULTI-AGENT ROUTING OF NEUROVASCULAR MICROROBOT SWARMS AT THE LIMIT This research monograph develops a falsifiable, non-clinical framework for routing heterogeneous microrobotic teams through branching neurovascular vessel phantoms. It asks whether decentralized task assignment, flow-aware navigation, independently tracked agent identity, and verifiable recovery can improve qualified sensing or inert-sample collection without increasing collision, occlusion, flow disturbance, thermal burden, sample confusion, or residual material risk. Organized around low-Reynolds-number hydrodynamics, multi-agent coordination, and independently enforced physical safety boundaries, the volume contains 30 mathematical derivation plates, 82 full research chapters with five separately paginated sections each, 200 detailed Research Gates, and 33 provisional Phoenix Answer Embryos. A DOI evidence ledger distinguishes established component physics and published demonstrations from the original system-level hypotheses proposed here. Strong passive-transport, single-agent, and information-matched centralized alternatives remain valid competitors throughout. Research failures, abandoned models, experimental uncertainty, and successor reconstruction are treated as scientific outputs, not editorial defects. The monograph provides a research architecture and prospective tests, not results from experiments performed for this publication. It does not assert demonstrated autonomous navigation in human cerebral vessels, clinical safety, therapeutic efficacy, or authorization for human intervention.

items.summary: AUTONOMOUS NANOROBOTIC NAVIGATION AND MISSION OBSERVABILITY AT THE LIMIT First-Generation Research Flagship 01 | NANO/MICRO ROBOTICS, POWER & MISSION ENDURANCE Feng Cheng-en (33) x Starli This research atlas asks a difficult engineering question: when low-Reynolds-number microfluidic flows, Brownian orientation noise, boundary adhesion, external field actuation and incomplete sensing all influence a micro/nanorobot, what would justify calling its behavior autonomous navigation rather than externally assisted motion? The volume treats navigation as an auditable, bounded mission instead of an attractive trajectory. It develops a five-layer program spanning stochastic hydrodynamics, instrument and actuation provenance, uncertainty-calibrated belief-state estimation, blinded microfluidic challenges and independent requalification. Thirty linked mathematical stations differentiate physical relations, information-theoretic functionals and proposed navigation utility measures, with assumptions, dimensions and possible falsifiers. Eighty-two research chapters each open with a core mathematical relation, followed by five independent single-page research sections. Two hundred detailed Research Gates describe decisive comparisons, confounding explanations, evidence requirements, failure conditions and successor handoff artifacts. Thirty-three provisional Phoenix Answer Embryos offer revisionable research prototypes rather than predetermined conclusions. The key comparator is an equal-budget experiment: fixed-field sequences, microscope-assisted manual control, externally tracked predictive control and candidate fused navigation are evaluated under matched total energy, information access, geometry, time, collision limits and recovery obligations. The manuscript emphasizes blind targets, flow reversal, sensor dropouts, wall adhesion, correlated observations, full-system power accounting, censored failures and post-mission retrieval. A mission arriving at its target but leaving an unrecovered device is not counted as a fully closed success. This work is a hypothesis-generating Research Atlas v1.0, not an experimental report or a validated medical technology. External magnetic, acoustic, optical and microscope infrastructure must be disclosed; no in-vivo or clinical competence is inferred from bench-top movement. Foundational DOI-linked literature provides context, not proof of the proposed integrated system. Every major claim is designed to be revised, rejected or reconstructed by a successor team using raw evidence and pre-registered falsification rules. Editorial release note: the manuscript prioritizes non-duplicative research content and independent testability over an artificial word-count target. items.summary: The underwater sound speed distribution directly governs acoustic propagation paths, rendering it critically important for underwater acoustic communication and target localization. Conventional sound speed profile (SSP) prediction methods provide a good way to estimate the underwater sound speed distribution without on-site data measurement, thus breaking through the coverage area constraints of sonar observation equipment and making the model universal in most marine areas. However, underwater sound speed exhibits multi-scale variations, such as diurnal, quarterly, and intermittent fluctuations caused by ocean processes such as internal waves. This makes it difficult for the fixed structure models in existing methods to have good generalization ability for multi-scale sound speed distribution patterns. To tackle this problem, we proposed a lightweight hybrid basis-function empowered Kolmogorov-Arnold network (LHBF-KAN) model for multi-scale sound speed prediction. We aim to construct a multi-branch representation layer in which different basis functions respond to distinct temporal patterns, from slowly varying background trends to rapid fluctuations induced by dynamic ocean processes, allowing the model to naturally accommodate the inherently multi-scale evolution of sound speed at different depths. To prevent the multi-branch structure from increasing model size, a pruning strategy is further introduced to suppress branches with consistently low contribution during training, yielding a compact architecture, suitable for deployment on resource constrained underwater platforms.
items.title: Robust Prediction of Internal Wave-Affected Multi-Scale Sound Speed Distribution Using Lightweight Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks with Hybrid Basis Functions

items.summary: Underwater acoustic target detection and recognition are essential to marine surveillance and intelligent ocean sensing. Despite substantial advances in deep learning, existing systems typically produce binary detection decisions, categorical labels, or scalar confidence scores, offering limited insight into the physical evidence underlying their outputs. Large language models (LLMs) offer an opportunity to move underwater acoustic sensing toward interpretable, evidence-grounded understanding; however, generic audio encoders struggle to capture the distinctive physical characteristics of underwater acoustics, and physically annotated data are scarce. In this paper, the first of a two-part series, we propose a from-signals-to-evidence framework that integrates physics-aware acoustic encoding with a pretrained LLM, organized around a unified feature-evidence-decision chain with a shared reasoning core. An open input layer accommodates heterogeneous information-raw waveforms, time-frequency representations, environmental and geographic data, and textual physical priors-unifying detection and recognition within a common formulation. In Part I, we instantiate this framework for target recognition through an Underwater Acoustic Physics-aware Transformer (UPT), which tokenizes complementary acoustic representations and learns task-disentangled physical representations through four physics-oriented learning tasks. We develop a physics-parameterized data engine that provides traceable supervision at two levels of granularity and introduce an attribute-level evaluation protocol to assess the physical fidelity of generated descriptions. Experiments on simulated recordings of four vessels demonstrate accurate vessel recognition and reliable estimation of shaft frequency, blade-passing frequency, and machinery-related attributes.
items.title: From Signals to Evidence: Interpretable Underwater Acoustic Target Sensing with Large Language Models - Part I: Framework and Recognition

items.summary: Version 2.0 is a substantive revision of version 1.0 (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.19174862). It supersedes the earlier procedural interpretation and its exclusion of competing explanations. The revised title is Structural Organization and Interpretive Limits of the Phaistos Disc. Reproduced descriptive findings are retained; failed model comparisons and photographic uncertainties are reported explicitly. The earlier version remains available through the record version history. We examine whether reproducible structural observations on the Phaistos Disc support a procedural interpretation. A pinned numerical transcription contains 242 main-sign positions, including one unreadable position, 45 readable sign types, 61 divider-defined groups and 18 supplementary stroke annotations. Source review reconciles counting and numbering conventions while retaining unresolved photographic uncertainty. The 02-to-12 side contrast persists after exact-family collapse. Adding side to a fixed position-only pairing predictor improves held-family loss by 0.082738 nats, but its exact conditional tail of 0.075 fails the frozen support rule. A positional mixture fails to outperform a bigram baseline. A separate directional test of the proposed 07-to-27 recovery relationship fails, with a one-sided permutation tail of 0.884. Supplementary-stroke comparisons have insufficient controlled overlap for the specified exact test. The work documents organization and constrains specific interpretations without establishing procedural functions or phonetic values. Corpus, code, protocols, full results and uncertainty ledgers accompany the paper.
items.title: Structural Organization and Interpretive Limits of the Phaistos Disc

items.summary: Adaptive modulation and coding (AMC) improves the spectral efficiency of underwater acoustic (UWA) links, but its feedback is inevitably stale: sound propagates slowly, and by the time channel state information (CSI) arrives, the fast time-varying multipath channel has moved on. Predictive link adaptation therefore needs more than a point forecast: it needs a distribution over each candidate action's consequences. We propose PRB-WM, a physics-regularized Beta world model for predictive per-subcarrier link adaptation on real time-varying UWA channels. A persistence-anchored stochastic latent-space dynamics model learns how the channel evolves; a counterfactual outcome head evaluates, for every candidate modulation and coding scheme (MCS), a Beta-binomial distribution of bit errors on shared imagined futures; and a chance-constrained receding-horizon model predictive controller maximizes expected spectral efficiency subject to a bounded probability of violating the bit error rate (BER) target. To the best of our knowledge, PRB-WM is the first world model for UWA communications. In closed-loop replay of six measured sea-trial links from the public UWA Channel Library against a 24-method pool spanning the full methodological spectrum, PRB-WM attains a mean goodput 87% above the strongest baseline, ranks first on all six time-varying links at the longest lookahead, and is the only method whose realized frame risk decreases systematically with lookahead, meeting the BER-violation contract where no baseline does. Ablations confirm that rollout sampling dispersion is essential to the chance constraint and that the physics anchor is necessary for trainability.
items.title: PRB-WM: Physics-Regularized Beta World Models for Predictive Link Adaptation on Real Time-Varying Underwater Acoustic Channels

items.summary: The Voynich Manuscript exhibits strong statistical regularities, but the distinction between recoverable grammar and recoverable lexical meaning remains unresolved. This study asks how far a progressively frozen, cross-validated analysis can reconstruct the manuscript’s internal word-building system without assigning meanings from illustrations, candidate languages, or post-hoc English paraphrase. Using canonical transcription, protected holdout partitions, alternate-transcription replication, exact host substitutions, and adversarial stopping rules, the analysis recovers a cumulative left-edge morphology, a transferable inventory of 39 surface CORE-0 stem/bodies, reproducible host-by-right-state coupling, a stable K/T referential contrast, and a directed network among powered lexical cores. The 39-core inventory predicts protected-frame combinatorics and content-blind contextual fingerprints out of sample, while attempts to decompose these bodies into a deeper transferable root layer fail. Nine recurring hosts show strongly replicated coupling to EY/EEY/EDY right-edge states, supporting a distributed morphological paradigm rather than independent left- and right-side systems. A 28-node directed CORE network also replicates across canonical calibration, untouched Holdout, and alternate-transcription tests, yielding neutral outbound- and inbound-biased stem classes without requiring part-of-speech or semantic assignments. On the project’s fully constrained 1,609-line benchmark, 12,299 of 12,495 positions are role-naturalizable (98.4314%), leaving 196 opaque positions. This percentage is explicitly a conditional benchmark-maturity statistic, not a measure of literal plaintext recovery or manuscript-wide translation accuracy. Repeated attempts to cross from structural organization to ordinary lexical meaning—including deeper-root induction, topic clustering, functional-neighborhood anchoring, local lexical syntax, illustration matching, source-language fitting, and prospective semantic transfer—fail the project’s promotion criteria. The resulting contribution is therefore a structural decipherment rather than a lexical one: a reproducible grammatical and morphological architecture together with an empirically identified lexical-identifiability ceiling. The work extends, but is distinct from, the earlier controlled-translation release at DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22049207.
items.title: Structural Decipherment Without Lexical Recovery: A Cross-Validated Morphological Analysis of the Voynich Manuscript

items.summary: Large audio-language models (LALMs) are fast becoming a general interface to sound, yet how far their broad pretraining carries into specialized domains remains largely open. Vessel monitoring, maritime safety, and ocean sensing all depend on recognizing underwater signals, but to our knowledge LALMs have not been systematically evaluated on them. Annotated recordings are costly to collect, and a faithful synthetic alternative has to bring together many interacting factors: the structure of detection pulses, communication waveforms, and ship-radiated noise, and the sound-speed profile, geometry, and multipath propagation through which each reaches the receiver. We address this by proposing \textbf{UA-Bench}, to our knowledge the first large-scale benchmark for evaluating LALMs on underwater acoustic signal recognition. It comprises 375,051 audio records that couple parameterized sources with modeled propagation, so that every record can be traced to the conditions that produced it. The records span these three signal families, and each carries a three-level label hierarchy (13 leaf classes), a templated multi-turn dialogue, and source and channel metadata. We evaluate on a balanced 2,600-record subset with a gated coarse-to-fine protocol that locates each error at source routing, fine-grained classification, or output format, and add a paired silent-audio control to test whether the waveform is actually used. Nine open LALMs, evaluated without task-specific adaptation, reach only 2.0\%--13.1\% leaf accuracy, against a random reference of 7.7\%. The waveform helps source routing far more than leaf recognition (for one model, +29.5 versus +2.3 points over silence), and just four models gain reliably at the leaf level, by at most 4.7 points. UA-Bench thus gives a reference point for these models, and its released training partition supports follow-up adaptation work.
items.title: UA-Bench: Benchmarking Large Audio-Language Models on Underwater Acoustic Recognition

items.summary: Semiconductor spin qubits offer a promising route to compact and scalable quantum computers, combining long coherence times in isotopically purified silicon with compatibility with semiconductor manufacturing. Beyond computational speedup, their energy efficiency is an important consideration for future large-scale systems. We evaluate the power and energy requirements of a Loss-DiVincenzo spin-qubit quantum computer by analyzing the Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT) and benchmarking it against the classical Fast Fourier Transform (FFT). We develop a detailed energy budget, identifying cryogenic cooling as the dominant baseline contribution before quantum error correction (QEC). The comparison between the QFT and the classical FFT reveals that, for any quantum workload operating under a polynomially bounded sampling regime, the crossover in energy consumption occurs at smaller problem sizes than the crossover in execution time. Thus, quantum computing can become energetically competitive before achieving a speedup in execution time. We then incorporate surface-code QEC and analyze the energy costs of QEC cycles, gate synthesis, and decoding. At scale, instrumentation and decoding become dominant contributions, while cryogenic cooling imposes a constraint on scalability. We show that optimizing the control-signal demultiplexing ratio can reduce the overall energy cost by approximately two orders of magnitude. For a system with about one million physical qubits, we estimate a power consumption of approximately 100 kW, at least one order of magnitude below that of today's highest-performance classical computing systems.
items.title: Energetics of Fault-Tolerant Spin-Qubit Quantum Computation

items.summary: Multi-head latent attention (MLA) compresses the content of a key-value cache into a shared latent per token, making low-bit storage attractive for long-context inference. At two bits, errors in this representation perturb both attention matching and value readout, with effects that depend on error direction and reconstruction scale. We introduce RoLaQ (Rotation-calibrated Latent Quantization), an offline method for joint rotation and range calibration. RoLaQ refines a shared rotation within subspaces defined by the frozen key and value projections, and jointly learns quantization ranges whose thresholds and reconstruction gains are coupled to control the shared signal's response. Prediction matching and attention-output supervision guide calibration with model weights frozen. Across three MLA models and six benchmarks, RoLaQ achieves the highest average accuracy among the compared 2-bit methods both without and with token protection. On DeepSeek-V2-Lite, an SGLang implementation provides 3.96 times the BF16 KV capacity under the same memory budget and 2.51 times its decode throughput with 256K input tokens.
items.title: RoLaQ: Joint Rotation and Range Calibration for 2-Bit KV Caches in Multi-Head Latent Attention

items.summary: Multi-agent collaboration has emerged as a critical paradigm for tackling complex, long-horizon tasks; however, while coordination protocols continue to advance, systemic failures at the inter-agent collaboration interface remain a pervasive bottleneck. In collaborative workflows, systems frequently suffer from \emph{broken handoffs}---where critical task context is omitted, misrouted, or ignored despite each agent emitting locally plausible responses. To address this challenge, we present \method, a verifiable runtime control framework that treats handoff repair as selective intervention over explicit dependency graphs. Central to \method is an integrated fault-attribution and calibration pipeline, \dataset, which decouples execution dependencies and injects counterfactual handoff perturbations to provide empirical supervision for runtime intervention. Leveraging this diagnostic foundation, \method dynamically compiles observable interaction traces into a provenance graph to pinpoint unresolved dependencies, without accessing private agent states. It then evaluates candidate repairs through an empirical gate that weighs expected gains against disruption risks, and executes repairs only when formal local postconditions hold. Extensive evaluations across demanding benchmarks demonstrate that \method boosts task success by up to 12.3 absolute percentage points on SILO-BENCH and 11.1 on TeamBench. Across both backbones, \method maintains strict cost-effectiveness, adding as little as 2.0\% marginal token overhead. Furthermore, on 562 handoff-relevant traces from the MAST benchmark, \method achieves 69.8\% F1 in a single pass, establishing a reliable operational boundary for verifiable coordination repair.
items.title: BRIDGE: Selective Boundary Repair with Dependency Graph Evidence in Multi-Agent Systems

Version 2.0.4 completes the regeneration path of the Supplementary Information: python reproduce.py baselines covers every size computed in the paper (ideal control up to twelve qubits), python reproduce.py symmetry also reports the symmetry fractions and compares the Holm-corrected p-values and partial correlations, python reproduce.py verify --exact repeats the dense validation, python reproduce.py replay retrains a paper run against its stored history, and the three runs of the propagation-cadence calibration are included (983 runs). items.summary: Few-shot adaptation often relies on an encoder's final global representation, leaving complementary information in intermediate layers underused. Combining these features is challenging because their dimensions can differ and their usefulness varies across tasks. We propose LAMP, Layerwise Adaptive Mixing of Predictors, a training-free framework that combines global and regional information from multiple encoder layers. A single forward pass per view supplies all descriptors. Global and support-calibrated regional kernel predictors independently fit the same label residuals. Labeled validation data select their mixture in class-score space, preserving native feature dimensions without learned projections. LAMP-F further adapts text-anchored class prototypes, using a cached response to update the fixed-kernel residual predictions exactly. Experiments cover eleven datasets and ViT and ResNet backbones. LAMP achieves state-of-the-art mean accuracy among the compared published training-free ResNet-50 methods at 4, 8, and 16 shots, reaching 78.73% at 16 shots. Averaged across five support budgets, LAMP improves over a paired global-feature-only baseline by 1.14 and 1.59 percentage points on ViT-B/16 and ResNet-50; LAMP-F raises these gains to 1.96 and 2.54 points. LAMP-F reaches 16-shot accuracies of 83.57% and 79.10%, respectively. Controlled experiments identify multi-layer integration as the main source of improvement and examine pooling, calibration, validation labels, and computational cost. These findings show that combining layer-specific predictions can exploit complementary features from frozen encoders to improve few-shot classification.
items.title: LAMP: Layerwise Adaptive Mixing of Predictors for Training-Free Few-Shot Vision-Language Adaptation

items.summary: Recent advances in deep learning have significantly improved underwater acoustic vessel recognition. However, existing publicly available datasets are typically limited in scale, hindering large-scale representation learning and downstream task evaluation. To address this limitation, we introduce ONCship, a large-scale underwater acoustic dataset comprising 4521 hours of curated recordings from Ocean Networks Canada (ONC) hydrophones and Automatic Identification System (AIS) data. We evaluate the proposed dataset across three tasks: self-supervised representation learning, vessel-type classification, and MMSI-Level Vessel Classification. Experiments on DeepShip and ShipsEar demonstrate the effectiveness of ONCship for acoustic representation learning, with joint pre-training on ONCship and AudioSet achieving a classification accuracy of 62.45% on DeepShip through linear probing. Furthermore, incorporating ONCship as auxiliary training data improves downstream vessel-type classification performance. Beyond conventional vessel-type classification, we further investigate MMSI-Level Vessel Classification, treating each vessel as a distinct identity. Experimental results show that models fine-tuned with different loss functions achieve Top-1 accuracies exceeding 53% and Top-5 accuracies approaching 69%, demonstrating the feasibility of distinguishing individual vessels through MMSI-Level Vessel Classification. Overall, ONCship provides a valuable resource for underwater acoustic representation learning and vessel recognition, while its rich vessel-level metadata enables further exploration of MMSI-Level Vessel Classification.
items.title: ONCship: A Large-Scale Underwater Acoustic Corpus for Ship Recognition

Changes in 1.0.1: two files with the per-identity counts of the exploratory published-measure analysis (file-based churn, cohort B; Supplementary Section S13 of the article) were added, re-keyed like the other cohort-B files; every file of version 1.0.0 is unchanged. The files are per-unit derived counts of the 3,687 cohort-A accounts and the cohort-B identities, with random identifiers (marker dates reduced to the month; no account names, e-mail addresses, repository names, commit SHAs or commit times). Placed by python3 reproduce.py --level2 <folder> of the Level-1 package (version 1.0.3), they recompute the registered aggregates and the exploratory aggregates that do not require the raw commit logs, including rates, transitions, paired contrasts, random-exclusion benchmarks and bootstrap intervals; on Python 3.10.12 with numpy 2.2.6 (Linux, aarch64) and on Python 3.13.16 with numpy 2.5.3 (Linux, x86_64) every regenerated result agreed with the reported one (numerical values within 1e-9, text files identical apart from line endings). Access is restricted because cohort-B rows keep the positions of their repositories in the public sampling order, which the registered repository-cluster bootstrap needs. Access is granted to researchers who state their name, affiliation and purpose and who agree to use the files only to verify, reproduce or extend the analyses of the article, not to redistribute the files or per-unit derivatives, not to attempt any re-identification or linkage to public commit histories or accounts, to store the files securely and delete them when the work is complete, and to cite the article and both archives (ACCESS.md). Reviewers of the article receive an access link through the editor.
items.title: Replication package (Level 2, restricted) for "Auditing successor selection in software repository mining: Evidence from filtering AI-attributed commits"

items.summary: Replication files for “Bans versus Controlled Access: Reserve Substitution and Issuer Buybacks under Financial Sanctions”. The A7A5 archive covers the TRON base contract TLeVfrdym8RoJreJ23dAGyfJDygRtiWKBZ from 7–27 August 2025 UTC. Data were retrieved on 17 October 2026 UTC. It includes 5,244 unique events from 37 daily response pages, additional event-class and receipt checks, frozen source responses and request provenance, event-level records, daily and weekly aggregates, supply accounting, data definitions, and analysis and verification scripts. Coverage is specific to the queried contract and provider. Gross transfers do not measure trading volume, beneficial ownership, reserve flows, or issuer buyback expenditure. The pilot is descriptive and does not identify a causal sanctions effect. The model archive contains Python scripts and supplied outputs for hypothetical numerical examples of route substitution, constrained issuer purchases, monitoring-dependent depth, surplus access and fallback. Parameters are not calibrated to A7A5. Both archives use Python 3.9 or later and its standard library; their README files give offline reproduction commands. Access: metadata are public; files are restricted and available on request to the corresponding author, hyoungkang@hanyang.ac.kr. The accompanying RIGHTS_AND_SOURCES.md distinguishes author-created materials from third-party responses. Rights in original materials are reserved; no blanket open license is granted for the mixed archive. The associated manuscript is unpublished.
items.title: A7A5 pilot data and model replication files for Bans versus Controlled Access

items.summary: We have presented a mathematically closed, comprehensive foundation for the C861 discrete spectral benchmark. By establishing the exact rank-two projector geometry, resolving Dirichlet sum cancellations, providing constructive proofs for linear B-spline KAN operator reproduction, and formalizing the Lyapunov convergence of Dense Associative Memory on spherical manifolds, this framework eliminates ambiguities in evaluating learned physical operators. Furthermore, the spectral interlacing analysis of the CN → PN structural homotopy equips the scientific machine learning community with a tool to distinguish authentic topological sensitivity from numerical discretization artifacts.
items.title: Exact Discrete Spectral Invariants as a Falsification Baseline for Learned Operator

items.summary: Key-value (KV) cache management has become a critical bottleneck for scaling Large Language Models (LLMs) to long-context scenarios due to linear memory growth. While recent eviction methods have moved beyond simple attention-score heuristics to incorporate value representations, they typically face a fundamental trade-off: the underlying optimization for minimizing output perturbation is an NP-hard combinatorial problem, leading to mathematically suboptimal heuristics or implementations that are difficult to kernelize. In this work, we propose DropKV, a simple principled eviction framework based on Decoupled Residual-Output Perturbation. By decoupling the joint eviction decision into independent per-token scoring, DropKV circumvents combinatorial intractability and admits a provable constant-factor approximation guarantee under a cone condition that we empirically verify on three long-context LLMs. To ensure practical viability, we provide a high-performance implementation using fused Triton kernels that avoid materializing the full attention matrix, delivering a 19.8x scoring-kernel speedup that translates to up to a 9.9% matched-batch end-to-end prefill speedup. Extensive evaluations on the RULER and LongBench benchmarks demonstrate that DropKV consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines at equivalent cache budgets, achieving the lowest inference latency among eviction methods while also remaining faster than the dynamic cache baseline.
items.title: DropKV: Decoupling Residual-Output Perturbation for Near-Optimal KV-Cache Eviction

items.summary: Weight-space learning across architectures requires representations that respect parameter symmetries and scale to large networks. Existing equivariant tensor encoders require architecture-specific symmetry specifications, while neuron graphs make global attention costly. We introduce a typed graph organized around shared coordinate-permutation actions. Its nodes, called interfaces, represent coordinate spaces whose bound tensor axes must be permuted jointly; operation occurrences, called modules, form typed hyperedges. A compiler derives this graph from supported PyTorch models, with exact recovery of the permutation factors defined by its constraints. The Universal Weight Encoder (UWE) combines local equivariant updates to parameter features with global attention over invariant interface summaries. The small number of interfaces makes global attention practical, and a single encoder processes different supported architectures. UWE is competitive with architecture-specific state-of-the-art methods on established benchmarks. On a new zoo of 1,200 transformers spanning 100 architectures, it outperforms the evaluated baselines at ranking networks within unseen architectures, including architectures larger than those used for training, while using substantially less memory.
items.title: Interfaces and Modules: A Scalable Representation for Weight-Space Learning across Architectures

items.summary: Pre-registration for a benchmark that tests whether frontier models can find struck-through text in documents as well as pdf-strikethrough-detect, an open-source package that detects struck-through text in PDFs and scanned pages, and at what cost. Ten models from Anthropic, Google, OpenAI and xAI run beside the package and two text-extraction baselines, on synthetic redlines, public redlined documents, US Congress bills and handwritten scans. This version holds the files tagged prereg-2, fixed after the dev runs and before any model sees a test page: PREREG.md: the rules, from the arms, inputs, prompts and scoring to the statistics, the four primary endpoints and the budget, now with the choices made on dev and the test run's cap. PLAN.md: the reasons behind them, unchanged since prereg-1. corpus_manifest.json: the source documents, each with its URL and sha256, unchanged. prereg1.json: what prereg-1 fixed, including the model IDs, page lists, file hashes and the prompts as drafted. prereg2.json: what prereg-2 fixes, including the sha256 of the code, prompts, config and every test page's ground truth, the choices made on dev, the model settings and the cap. PREREG.md sha256: 3d3c5d44579eeeae387660d682f6bcab8016b48dc048442634c16eeb7a22bcbc The same files are in the package's GitHub release prereg-2. Since prereg-1, PREREG.md has changed only by the values the dev runs chose and by three logged deviations.
items.title: Frontier benchmark for pdf-strikethrough-detect: pre-registration 2

items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents solve complex tasks by calling external tools over multiple turns. Recent work has proposed tool graph memory, which stores past experience as tool transitions to guide subsequent selection. However, it remains unclear whether this component consistently improves agents' tool use or undermines it. We evaluate tool graph memory on nine models and two benchmarks, finding that it seldom improves significantly over baselines, and that its gains, where present, cost over twice the LLM calls. The memory's guidance is often incorrect, and random or no guidance retains most of the gain, implying that the benefit stems from extra computation rather than the memory itself. Moreover, even with the correct next tool suggested, many failures remain, such as giving up without a tool call. Storing the same experience instead as textual insights outperforms tool graph memory with almost no extra LLM calls. This suggests that memory serves better as a soft prior than as a prescription of the next tool, leading to a more effective and generalizable solution.
items.title: Rethinking the Role of Tool Graph Memory in Multi-Turn Tool Use

items.summary: Long-horizon multi-agent collaboration requires memory that preserves both successful actions and the coordination structure underlying them. Existing memory systems support information sharing or procedural reuse, but often leave the evolution of shared procedures disconnected from the task dependencies and execution states of collaborating agents. This coupling also limits the direct transfer of procedural memory designed for individual agents to team settings. We propose Self-Evolving Procedural Memory (SEPM), a framework that uses task dependency graphs as a common representation for online coordination and procedural memory evolution. During execution, a lightweight shared blackboard records structured evidence alongside task dependencies, supporting the detection of goal, plan, and world-state divergence and evidence-based realignment. After execution, verified actions and dependencies are distilled into reusable procedures, while recurring failures inform warnings and constraints. The shared procedure pool evolves through creation, refinement, specialization, and retirement, guided by success and cost utility and constrained by evidence and safety requirements. Together, these mechanisms preserve the collaborative structure and applicability conditions needed to reuse experience across tasks. Evaluations on ALFWorld, WebArena, and OfficeBench under AutoGen and DyLAN show that SEPM achieves the highest task scores among the compared methods in all six benchmark settings. Under AutoGen, it improves task scores over the no-added-memory baseline by 29.85, 25.86, and 13.00 percentage points, respectively. The codebase is available at https://github.com/cookieApril/SEPM.
items.title: SEPM: Self-Evolving Procedural Memory Grounded in Task Graphs for Multi-Agent Collaboration

items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents can self-evolve at test time by accumulating experience: retrieving relevant memories before acting and writing new lessons back afterwards. Yet most are single-level: trajectories, distilled workflows and reasoning items all land in one undifferentiated pool indexed by embedding similarity, with no typed abstraction hierarchy. They never forget or deduplicate, and are prone to negative transfer, where a superficially similar but directionally opposite experience is recalled and its concrete steps are copied verbatim, actively harming the agent. We introduce STRATA, a structured, outcome-grounded, self-maintaining memory that organizes experience into a three-layer graph of atomic skills and code snippets, task workflows and generalized meta-frameworks, connected by typed edges. STRATA maintains itself through five mechanisms sharing one similarity geometry: a multi-dimensional similarity that scores retrieval by operation and target; a typed reflector crystallizing procedures from successes and pitfalls from failures; community detection that induces meta-frameworks; pressure-triggered garbage collection with articulation-point protection; and contrast edges that flag confusable, direction-opposite experiences. Across four interactive benchmarks (AppWorld, WebArena, ALFWorld, ScienceWorld), two frozen backbones and seven baselines, STRATA attains the best average score while simultaneously using the lowest latency and fewest environment steps of any memory-augmented method, and 44% fewer lines of injected memory than the most context-hungry baseline. We isolate two failure modes of prior memories: single-level memory degrades sharply as the task set grows, and single-level concrete memories suffer catastrophic negative transfer, which contrast edges repair, lifting ScienceWorld from 78.7 to 96.7 within the same system.
items.title: STRATA: Self-Maintaining Structured Experience Graphs for Self-Evolving Language Agents

items.summary: As Vision-Language Models (VLMs) advance, they are increasingly expected to perform spatiotemporal reasoning over motion, actions, and view changes beyond what the input images show. Video World Models (VWMs) provide a natural unified engine for visual imagination by generating task-relevant visual content as additional evidence. However, existing approaches typically invoke a VWM through fixed pipelines centered on a predefined form of visual imagination, such as novel-view synthesis. To support flexible visual imagination for diverse reasoning tasks, we introduce CoWorld Reasoner, an agentic framework that uses a VWM as a unified visual reasoning engine. Its Video World Model-Driven Harness exposes multiple visual operations through tools and uses skills to guide the VLM in deciding whether to imagine, selecting an operation, constructing a generation request, and interpreting the resulting visual evidence. We further introduce VLM-VWM Harness Co-Evolution, which jointly revises tools, skills, and execution code based on execution feedback while keeping both model weights fixed. Across seven benchmarks spanning spatial intelligence, temporal and causal reasoning, and perceptual reasoning, CoWorld Reasoner outperforms direct reasoning with the same VLM. The strongest variant improves on all seven benchmarks, including relative accuracy gains of 11.8% on MMSI and 13.0% on ERQA, and outperforms all five evolving baselines using the same backbone across five benchmarks.
items.title: CoWorld Reasoner: Agentic Multimodal Reasoning with the Evolving Video World Model-Driven Harness

items.summary: Singing Accompaniment Generation (SAG) is the process of generating instrumental music for a given clean vocal input. However, existing SAG techniques use source-separated vocals as input and overfit to separation artifacts. This creates a critical train-test mismatch, leading to failure on clean, real-world vocal inputs. We introduce AnyAccomp, a framework that resolves this by decoupling accompaniment generation from source-dependent artifacts. AnyAccomp first employs a quantized melodic bottleneck, using a chromagram and a VQ-VAE to extract a discrete and timbre-invariant representation of the core melody. A subsequent flow-matching model then generates the accompaniment conditioned on these robust codes. Experiments show AnyAccomp achieves competitive performance on separated-vocal benchmarks while significantly outperforming baselines on generalization test sets of clean studio vocals and, notably, solo instrumental tracks. This demonstrates a qualitative leap in generalization, enabling robust accompaniment for instruments - a task where existing models completely fail - and paving the way for more versatile music co-creation tools. Demo audio and code: https://anyaccomp.github.io
items.title: AnyAccomp: Generalizable Accompaniment Generation via Quantized Melodic Bottleneck
